title: Creating a trading strategy and platform using Claude and GPT
author: LogicVoyager7
selftext: i want to create a trading strategy and platform which i can use to paper trade and backtest ( only for now ). I wont be using any real money to trade and will only test different strategies everyday. For this im thinking to use claude and gpt to do research, implement the complex strategies, data, coding and logic. Since i will be starting it from scratch, so i wanted to ask everyone here who has been currently doing this for long and also some suggestions which i should take care of before starting it. The main point here is i wont be doing real money trading which means its just for my educational purpose.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Either one can write the code, and I wouldn't spend much time choosing between them. What matters more is how you check the work, since AI-written backtests often have small mistakes, like using tomorrow's data today or leaving out fees. I'd start with one simple strategy, test it with fees and slippage included, and keep a stretch of data aside that you never tune on. Having the AI explain each step so you can follow the logic also helps. If you want a ready-made place to test before building your own, Cymetica's Backtest Labs runs bots on past data with a fee setting.

comments.author: LaysWellWithOthers
comments.body:
The labs are all competing against one another and things move quickly, as such identifying which one is best today does not mean it will be best tomorrow.

I've been building an agentic trading platform on and off for the last 18 months and I have used both throughout. 

I use an adversarial approach where I have one model as the executor and the other as the reviewer (I am the operator) this pattern persists throughout the whole lifecycle. 

The good news is that both are very much capable of doing this individually, the bad news is that building it is the easy part, finding an edge is extremely challenging.

comments.author: chikeez
comments.body:
Starting on paper only is the right call imo, and both models will write the code fine. Pick whichever one’s code you find easier to read, because you’ll be reading a lot lol. I think the bigger risk is in your plan itself: testing a different strategy every day.

Here’s why. Say you try 20 strategies with no edge at all, each a coin flip that wins or loses 1R, and run each for 50 trades. On average, the best of the 20 finishes around +12R, a 62% win rate. It looks like a real find, and it’s pure luck. I simulated this, and the result holds.

So keep a log of every strategy you try, including the ones you drop. A winner that’s the best of 3 means far more than the best of 30. Before you trust a winner, run it again on the next month of paper trades with no changes. Most lucky ones fall apart there.

If you're gonna build one thing first, make it that log.

replies.author: LogicVoyager7
replies.body: Thanks. That log idea is indeed better to track

comments.author: Key-Enthusiasm-3403
comments.body:
i built a paper trading game with claude and the two things that mattered most weren't the strategy code



first, never let the data fail over to something made up. if the price feed drops, mine refuses to run and says why, because one run on fake prices makes every result after it meaningless and you won't remember which ones were affected



second, put costs in from day one, a spread and a fee on every fill. paper fills are always cleaner than real ones, so a sim without costs flatters everything you test



on claude vs gpt i'd agree with the others, either writes it fine. what i'd add is have the model write a check as well as the code, a test with a day where you already know the right answer

comments.author: Sure-Function7604
comments.body: what kind of strategies are you trying to test? Like do you want to use fundamental data (financial metrics), or technical indicators? or both? Is this day trading, swing trading, or long term investing?

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
Claude writes the cleaner code in my experience, but the model matters less than the checks around it. either one will happily write a backtest that trades on the close of the bar it's reading, so write a look-ahead test before your first strategy.

that check sits under everything in the backtester I built, Quantradin. free, you type the rule in plain English, it grades it on history and runs it on fake money. quantradin.com

what are you planning to test first?

comments.author: ALGORA1-
comments.body:
The issue with using Claude or ChatGPT to build a qunatitiaive straeegy is that it doesn't have access to real time market data. Creating a strategy that passes the necessary rigorous tests needs data these LLMs cannot access such as point in time universe for over 12,000 tickers cover 20+ years of data.

replies.author: AssMan2025
replies.body: On Schwab Claude can pull history with a python command

replies.author: ALGORA1-
replies.body:
That's a useful approach, and Schwab's API can certainly help retrieve historical OHLCV data. However, there's a distinction between accessing historical prices and having the underlying datasets necessary to conduct rigorous quantitative research.

For example, how would you reconstruct the investable universe of 12,000+ U.S. stocks and ETFs as it existed 10, 15, or 20 years ago? How would you account for delisted companies, historical ticker changes, corporate actions, and survivorship bias?

That's the bigger challenge. An LLM can write the Python code to execute a backtest, but it cannot compensate for missing or incomplete historical datasets.

comments.author: tsh_m
comments.body:
Create idea if you truly want to start studying how some other strategies function bar by bar. I started building mine a few year ago with c++ before i even knew about AI, But now i can have either claude code or code manage the full engine, start/pause replays, take snapshots, explain what i am looking at, automate optimization, endless possibilities.

  
For which one to choose you might as well flip a coin, both of them are good but if you are going to optimize years of data or have your backtester read tick data, i would recommend GPT. In my opinion, Codex is very efficient with token usage, i can spend hours with their highest model and it can optimize strategies really fast, however, it always looking for the fastest way to reach its goal, if you love you coding style say bye bye, codex will only format your script with only few lines so as to not use many tokens(you ask code to reach a mountain it will be there in just a second).

  
Claude on the other hand is a different beast, you ask it to reach a mountain, it ask you how to you want it to do it, should i use a plane? a car? walk there?. At the end the results it going to be what you asked for, but at the cost of tokens. For optimizing large data, it will work very hard to provide good results, but sometimes it just used a lot of tokens for the same results as GPT, its very good at following the right path, which is not always the shortest path.

  
I would recommend both if you have enough to spend, one for coding(Claude), one for optimizing, brainstorming and other things(GPT).
